    5.2 File Handling

    Last updated on 2026-11-03 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 50 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I save data and read it back later?

    Objectives

    • Read and write text files with open() and with.
    • Read and write JSON and CSV files.

    File Handling

    So far we have seen different Python data types. We usually store our data in different file formats. In addition to handling files, we will also see different file formats(.txt, .json, .xml, .csv, .tsv, .excel) in this section. First, let us get familiar with handling files with common file format(.txt).

    File handling is an import part of programming which allows us to create, read, update and delete files. In Python to handle data we use open() built-in function.

    PYTHON 

    # Syntax
open('filename', mode) # mode(r, a, w, x, t,b)  could be to read, write, update
    • “r” - Read - Default value. Opens a file for reading, it returns an error if the file does not exist
    • “a” - Append - Opens a file for appending, creates the file if it does not exist
    • “w” - Write - Opens a file for writing, creates the file if it does not exist
    • “x” - Create - Creates the specified file, returns an error if the file exists
    • “t” - Text - Default value. Text mode
    • “b” - Binary - Binary mode (e.g. images)

    Opening Files for Reading

    The default mode of open is reading, so we do not have to specify ‘r’ or ‘rt’. I have created and saved a file named reading_file_example.txt in the files directory. Let us see how it is done:

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
print(f) # <_io.TextIOWrapper name='./files/reading_file_example.txt' mode='r' encoding='UTF-8'> - the encoding may differ on your computer
f.close()

    As you can see in the example above, I printed the opened file and it gave some information about it. Opened file has different reading methods: read(), readline, readlines. An opened file has to be closed with close() method.

    • read(): read the whole text as string. If we want to limit the number of characters we want to read, we can limit it by passing int value to the read(number) method.

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
txt = f.read()
print(type(txt))
print(txt)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'str'>
This is an example to show how to open a file and read.
This is the second line of the text.

    Instead of printing all the text, let us print the first 10 characters of the text file.

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
txt = f.read(10)
print(type(txt))
print(txt)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'str'>
This is an
    • readline(): read only the first line

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
line = f.readline()
print(type(line))
print(line)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'str'>
This is an example to show how to open a file and read.
    • readlines(): read all the text line by line and returns a list of lines

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
lines = f.readlines()
print(type(lines))
print(lines)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'list'>
['This is an example to show how to open a file and read.\n', 'This is the second line of the text.']

    Another way to get all the lines as a list is using splitlines():

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
lines = f.read().splitlines()
print(type(lines))
print(lines)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'list'>
['This is an example to show how to open a file and read.', 'This is the second line of the text.']

    After we open a file, we should close it. There is a high tendency of forgetting to close them. There is a new way of opening files using with - closes the files by itself. Let us rewrite the previous example with the with method:

    PYTHON 

    with open('./files/reading_file_example.txt') as f:
    lines = f.read().splitlines()
    print(type(lines))
    print(lines)

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'list'>
['This is an example to show how to open a file and read.', 'This is the second line of the text.']

    Opening Files for Writing and Updating

    To write to an existing file, we must add a mode as parameter to the open() function:

    • “a” - append - will append to the end of the file, if the file does not exist it creates a new file.
    • “w” - write - will overwrite any existing content, if the file does not exist it creates.

    The code below creates a new file, if the file does not exist:

    PYTHON 

    with open('./files/writing_file_example.txt','w') as f:
    f.write('This text will be written in a newly created file.\n')

    Now let us append some text to the end of that file. Running this again adds the line again, because “a” never removes what is already there:

    PYTHON 

    with open('./files/writing_file_example.txt','a') as f:
    f.write('This text has to be appended at the end.\n')

with open('./files/writing_file_example.txt') as f:
    print(f.read())

    OUTPUT 

    This text will be written in a newly created file.
This text has to be appended at the end.

    Deleting Files

    To remove a file we use the os module. Modules are explained in Week 6, so for now leave the import os line as is.

    PYTHON 

    import os
os.remove('./files/writing_file_example.txt')

    If the file does not exist, the remove method will raise an error, so it is good to use a condition like this:

    PYTHON 

    import os
if os.path.exists('./files/writing_file_example.txt'):
    os.remove('./files/writing_file_example.txt')
else:
    print('The file does not exist')
# The file does not exist - we already removed it above

    File Types

    File with txt Extension

    File with txt extension is a very common form of data and we have covered it in the previous section. Let us move to the JSON file

    File with json Extension

    JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation. Actually, it is a stringified JavaScript object or Python dictionary.

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    # dictionary
person_dct = {
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}

# JSON: the same data as a string. JSON always uses double quotes
person_json = '{"name": "Jack", "country": "Australia", "city": "Perth", "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]}'

# we use three quotes and make it multiple line to make it more readable
person_json = '''{
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}'''

    Changing JSON to Dictionary

    To change a JSON to a dictionary, first we import the json module and then we use loads method.

    PYTHON 

    import json
# JSON
person_json = '''{
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}'''
# let's change JSON to dictionary
person_dct = json.loads(person_json)
print(type(person_dct))
print(person_dct)
print(person_dct['name'])

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'dict'>
{'name': 'Jack', 'country': 'Australia', 'city': 'Perth', 'skills': ['Python', 'Excel', 'SQL']}
Jack

    Changing Dictionary to JSON

    To change a dictionary to a JSON we use dumps method from the json module.

    PYTHON 

    import json
# python dictionary
person = {
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}
# let's convert it to  json
person_json = json.dumps(person, indent=4) # indent could be 2, 4, 8. It beautifies the json
print(type(person_json))
print(person_json)

    When you print it, it does not have the quotes, but it is a string. JSON does not have its own type in Python: it is a string.

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'str'>
{
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": [
        "Python",
        "Excel",
        "SQL"
    ]
}

    Saving as JSON File

    We can also save our data as a json file. Let us save it as a json file using the following steps. For writing a json file, we use the json.dump() method, it can take dictionary, output file, ensure_ascii and indent.

    PYTHON 

    import json
# python dictionary
person = {
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}
with open('./files/json_example.json', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    json.dump(person, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=4)

    In the code above, we use encoding and indentation. Indentation makes the json file easy to read.

    File with csv Extension

    CSV stands for comma separated values. CSV is a simple file format used to store tabular data, such as a spreadsheet or database. CSV is a very common data format in data science.

    Example:

    "name","country","city","skills"
"Jack","Australia","Perth","Python"

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    import csv
with open('./files/csv_example.csv') as f:
    csv_reader = csv.reader(f, delimiter=',') # we use, reader method to read csv
    line_count = 0
    for row in csv_reader:
        if line_count == 0:
            print(f'Column names are :{", ".join(row)}')
            line_count += 1
        else:
            print(
                f'\t{row[0]} is a student. He lives in {row[2]}, {row[1]}.')
            line_count += 1
    print(f'Number of lines:  {line_count}')

    OUTPUT 

    Column names are :name, country, city, skills
        Jack is a student. He lives in Perth, Australia.
Number of lines:  2

    File with xlsx Extension

    To read Excel files we need to install the openpyxl package. Installing packages with pip is covered in Week 6, so for now just read this example; it will not run until openpyxl is installed.

    PYTHON 

    import openpyxl
workbook = openpyxl.load_workbook('sample.xlsx')
print(workbook.sheetnames)   # the names of the sheets, e.g. ['Sheet1']

    File with xml Extension

    XML is another structured data format which looks like HTML. In XML the tags are not predefined. The first line is an XML declaration. The person tag is the root of the XML. The person has a gender attribute. Example:XML

    XML 

    <?xml version="1.0"?>
<person gender="male">
  <name>Jack</name>
  <country>Australia</country>
  <city>Perth</city>
  <skills>
    <skill>Python</skill>
    <skill>Excel</skill>
    <skill>SQL</skill>
  </skills>
</person>

    For more information on how to read an XML file check the documentation

    PYTHON 

    import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
tree = ET.parse('./files/xml_example.xml')
root = tree.getroot()
print('Root tag:', root.tag)
print('Attribute:', root.attrib)
for child in root:
    print('field:', child.tag)

    OUTPUT 

    Root tag: person
Attribute: {'gender': 'male'}
field: name
field: country
field: city
field: skills
    Challenge

    1. Write a function which count number of lines and number of words in a text. All the files are in the data the folder:

      1. Read obama_speech.txt file and count number of lines and words
      2. Read michelle_obama_speech.txt file and count number of lines and words
      3. Read donald_speech.txt file and count number of lines and words
      4. Read melina_trump_speech.txt file and count number of lines and words

    2. Read the countries_data.json data file in data directory, create a function that finds the ten most spoken languages

      OUTPUT

(45, 'French'),

(45, 'French'),
(25, 'Arabic')]

    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 2

    1. Extract all incoming email addresses as a list from the email_exchange_big.txt file.
    2. Find the most common words in the English language. Call the name of your function find_most_common_words, it will take two parameters - a string or a file and a positive integer, indicating the number of words. Your function will return an array of tuples in descending order. Check the output

    OUTPUT 

        # Your output should look like this
    print(find_most_common_words('sample.txt', 10))
    [(10, 'the'),
    (8, 'be'),
    (6, 'to'),
    (6, 'of'),
    (5, 'and'),
    (4, 'a'),
    (4, 'in'),
    (3, 'that'),
    (2, 'have'),
    (2, 'I')]

    # Your output should look like this
    print(find_most_common_words('sample.txt', 5))

    [(10, 'the'),
    (8, 'be'),
    (6, 'to'),
    (6, 'of'),
    (5, 'and')]
    1. Use the function, find_most_frequent_words to find:
      1. The ten most frequent words used in Obama’s speech
      2. The ten most frequent words used in Michelle’s speech
      3. The ten most frequent words used in Trump’s speech
      4. The ten most frequent words used in Melina’s speech
    2. Write a python application that checks similarity between two texts. It takes a file or a string as a parameter and it will evaluate the similarity of the two texts. For instance check the similarity between the transcripts of Michelle’s and Melina’s speech. You may need a couple of functions, function to clean the text(clean_text), function to remove support words(remove_support_words) and finally to check the similarity(check_text_similarity). List of stop words are in the data directory
    3. Find the 10 most repeated words in the romeo_and_juliet.txt
    4. Read the hacker news csv file and find out:
      1. Count the number of lines containing python or Python
      2. Count the number lines containing JavaScript, javascript or Javascript
      3. Count the number lines containing Java and not JavaScript
    Key Points
    • Use with open(…) so the file closes itself.
    • Mode “w” overwrites, “a” appends, “r” reads.
    • json.dump() and json.load() save and load Python data.
